newsitem.title: USA: Retailers report solid sales gains for June.
newsitem.headline: Retailers report solid sales gains for June.

text.p: Warm weather boosted sales for many of the nation's largest retailers in June, but lackluster clothing sales hurt profits of a few merchants, the companies said Thursday.
Department stores and discount stores posted strong results after a heat wave and merchandise markdowns spurred shoppers to buy.

Wal-Mart Stores Inc., Kmart Corp. and Target, a unit of Dayton Hudson Corp., all reported better profits. Sales of fans, air conditioners and other seasonal goods picked up late in the month, which ended in early July for accounting purposes. The industry counted the first week this month, including the Independence Day holiday, in the results for June.
However, Kmart and a few speciality retailers, including AnnTaylor Stores Corp., said profits wilted because of poor apparel sales during the heat wave.
"Certainly, business got better when the weather got better," said Michael Exstein of Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "But sales were not robust for the industry."
An index compiled by Prudential Securities of same-store sales, or sales among stores open at least a year, rose 4.5 percent in June after climbing 4.3 percent during the same month last year.
"This is pretty much what we would have anticipated given the growth in the economy," said Prudential analyst Wayne Hood, noting the increase was in line with his expectations.
"If sales had risen more than 5 percent, people would be concerned the economy was gaining momentum and the Fed was going to raise rates."
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at its policy-making meeting last week amid signs of steady economic growth with few inflationary pressures.
Women's apparel was the weak spot for several speciality chains.

AnnTaylor Stores Corp. said same-store sales fell 5.8 percent and earnings in the second quarter would be disappointing. The company blamed "fashion misses" and lack of sufficient inventory to meet demand for the sales decline.
Earlier this week, Talbots Inc. said sales dropped 7.9 percent and warned it would report a net loss of $9 million to $12 million in the second quarter ending Aug. 2.

Limited Inc.'s sales grew 4 percent, but it came mostly from its Intimate Brands Inc. lingerie division and not from its women's apparel chains, including Express, where business was poor, analysts said.
While Kmart's sales were up 5.3 percent in June, it said it expected profits would fall below earnings of $34 million, or 7 cents a share in the 1996 second quarter.
"While sales of women's apparel improved slightly during June, clearance markdowns continue to be significantly higher than plan," Kmart Chairman Floyd Hall said in a statement issued late Wednesday.
Other chains were more upbeat. Federated Department Stores Inc., parent of Bloomingdale's, Macy's and Rich's, said it was "satisfied" with its 3.2 percent sales gain.

Kohl's Corp., a moderately priced department store, reported sales rose by 14.1 percent. "As summer weather finally arrived, it brought with it strong sales in all of our markets," said Kohl's Chairman William Kellogg.

May Department Stores Co., parent of Lord & Taylor, Foley's and Robinsons-May, said its sales rose 4.6 percent. Wal-Mart's sales rose by 6.4 percent, and Sears, Roebuck and Co. said its sales were up 3.1 percent.
